articles.title: Bye, live regions. Hello, ariaNotify()
articles.description: In September 2026, ariaNotify() was introduced as a new web API method to replace live regions. We...
articles.body_html:
In September 2026, ariaNotify() was introduced as a new web API method to replace live regions. We are going to learn when we have to use it, which compliance criteria it meets and its benefits.

Hello, ariaNotify() method!! The title might be a clickbait, because we are far from replacing live regions, buuut... I am super excited about this new feature. I have been waiting for it since 2024 when it was announced in the WAI-ARIA 1.3 draft and it finally becomes baseline, in September of this year (2026) having complete support on Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari. So, you might be wondering why the hype, let's find out.

What is ariaNotify()? It is a web API's method that was presented as a programmatic way to trigger screen reader announcements. Yes, same thing as live regions, but the main difference is that live regions are attached to a DOM element and to achieve this now we have to inject hidden text into a DOM element where the change lives, therefore it only announces a text when there is a structural modification on the content. On the contrary, ariaNotify() queues the text to be announced by screen readers using JavaScript.

Markup of Live Regions

A summary of how live regions works nowadays. They need a combination of HTML + CSS + JavaScript to work properly.

<!-- an empty DOM element -->
<p role="status"></p>

// Then, injects the upate on the empty DOM element
const region = document.querySelector('[role="status"]')
region.textContent = '3 results'

Roles

  • role="status": it is used for text that are advisory and not important enough to interrupt. It implies aria-live="polite" and aria-atomic="true".
  • role="alert": it is used for important and/or time-sensitive text and it interrupts what the screen reader is currently saying. It implies aria-live="assertive" and aria-atomic="true".
  • role="log": it is used for new entries in order, like a chat or live updates. It implies aria-live="polite".

WAI-ARIA

  • aria-live: it has three values, polite which waits until the user is idle, assertive which interrupts what the user is perceiving, off which indicates that the changes on a region will only be announced when the user focuses on it.
  • aria-atomic: its value can be true which means that the whole region will be announced when any part of it changes, or false which means that only the part of the region that changes is announced, for example, a clock going from 17.33 to 17.34, only the “34” will be announced.
  • aria-busy: it is used on live regions that might be modified to let the user know when they have been modified. Its value can be true which tells the screen reader that it may wait until the changes are finished before announcing them, or false which means that nothing happens and nothing will be announced until the task is finished.
  • aria-relevant: it is an optional attribute of live regions and it is just a suggestion to assistive technologies. Its values can be additions which refers to element nodes that are added to the accessibility tree within the live region, all, which it is a shorthand for additions removals text, removals which refers to any text content within the live region that is removed from the accessibility tree, or text which refers to text content or a text alternative that is added to any descendant in the accessibility tree of the live region.

Markup of ariaNotify() 


element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.', { priority: 'high' })
  1. Host element or document It is the element that will contain the announcement. It could be the Element in the accessibility tree, or the Document.
  2. Method ariaNotify() The method itself. It is called on the host and it contains the announcement and the options.
  3. Announcement 'Draft saved.' Required. It is the announcement text. Without it there is a TypeError.
  4. Options { priority: 'high' } Optional. If it is omitted or a value that is not on the dictionary is being placed, the value by default would be ‘normal’.
  5. Priority priority: 'high' | 'normal' normal, the default, is spoken after what is being spoken; high interrupts it.

Parallels with Live Regions

In Live Region In ariaNotify Parallelism
role="status", aria-live="polite" { priority: 'normal' } (the default) Both are polite regions and wait until the previous announcement has finished before announcing.
role="alert", aria-live="assertive" { priority: 'high' } Both interrupt what is being spoken to announce the latest message.
element.textContent = 'Draft saved.' element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.') The message to be announced.
aria-atomic="true" announcement text aria-atomic makes a whole region announceable when any part of it changes. In live regions it is applicable to the hidden string to announce but in ariaNotify the announcement text is already the argument to announce

Live Region 

<p role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true"></p>

<p role="alert" aria-atomic="true"></p>

const polite = document.querySelector('[role="status"]')
const assertive = document.querySelector('[role="alert"]')

polite.textContent = 'Draft saved.'
assertive.textContent = 'Could not save the draft.'

ariaNotify() 

<button type="button" lang="en">Save draft</button>

const element = document.querySelector('button')

element.ariaNotify('Draft saved.')
element.ariaNotify('Could not save the draft.', {
  priority: 'high',
})

In my opinion, the ariaNotify arrived to simplify the knowledge around announcements. In the past, having to communicate the knowledge about live regions was the biggest challenge for accessibility experts so having a method that with a single line of code covered the screen reader announcements without without hardcoding hidden text is refreshing.

Live Regions vs ariaNotify(): Use Cases

In this section, we will learn with use case examples how ariaNotify() simplifies the work and meets the WCAG success criterion to be compliant.

Here you can test the examples

Should I Document or Should I Element?

Neither of the MDN page for ariaNotify() in Document nor the MDN page for ariaNotify() in Element make a clear distinction between whether to attach the ariaNotify method to the Document or to the Element, but we can state that the choice is about the message per se. Based on that, I created the following table to help decide where to attach the method based on semantics and context.

Another thing worth mentioning is that the language of the announcement by default is, it comes from the lang attribute on the html element. If you want a dedicated section of the page to have a different language, set it explicitly.

Situation Where Why
Announcement about connection, a new version, session update, and a total upate Document The announcement is not tied to an action by the user or to an update in a region, but to a global update that improves or modifies the experience.
Announcement about a thing happening in a section of the page. It could be a count, a total updated, a progress bar, etc Element The announcement has a context, a scope
Announcement of something that has been removed from the DOM Document The Element does no longer exists in the DOM, so the announcement should be made from the Document

Reusable and Global Solution for Announcements Using Just ariaNotify()

In my lib of methods, last month I implemented a reusable function to dispatch announcements programmatically using the ariaNotify() method.

  1. A function to check if the native HTML element supports ariaNotify() 
   export const hasAriaNotify = () =>
     typeof Element !== 'undefined' && 'ariaNotify' in Element.prototype
  1. Create a type (if you are using TypeScript) to tell TypeScript the method may exist and what it takes. 
   type Notifier = {
      ariaNotify?: (announcement: string, options?: { priority: Priority }) => void
    }
  1. Then we have to create a notify function 
   export function notify(
      from: Element | Document,
      message: string,
      priority: Priority = 'normal',
    ) {
      const native = hasAriaNotify()
      const send = () => {
        (from as unknown as Notifier).ariaNotify?.(message, { priority })
      }
      if (native) return send()
    }
  • The function has 3 mandatory parameters: from which checks if the method is being attached to an Element or Document, message which is the string of texts to be announced and priority which is the type of announcement that the screen reader should do.
  • If native is true, we are going to attach the method to the Element/Document and dispatch the action.
    1. The reusable function can be used in the following way: 
   notify(bar, 'report.pdf uploaded.')

Screen Readers

Click here to discover how screen readers announce the announcements of ariaNotify method

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion - Level AA

Success Criterion Explanation
4.1.3 Status Messages (AA) as in Technique ARIA27, the progress should be announced.
3.3.1 Error Identification (A) For example, a failed upload should be announced with high priority

Browser Support

According to MDN, this is the list of browsers that support ariaNotify on their latest update since September 2026. Oldest versions might not support ariaNotify.

  • Chrome version 141
  • Edge version 141
  • Firefox version 150
  • Opera version 125
  • Safari version 27
  • Chrome Android version 141
  • Firefox Android version 150
  • Opera Android version 93
  • Safari on iOS version 27
  • Samsung Browser version 30
  • WebView Android version 141
  • WebView on iOS version 27

Resources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/ariaNotify
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/ariaNotify
  • https://w3c.github.io/aria/#ARIANotifyMixin

articles.title: Napsha: Testing a Claude Skill for Open Inquiry into AI Subjectivity
articles.description: description: "Building an open-source inquiry skill, comparing Claude responses, and learning to...
articles.body_html:
description: "Building an open-source inquiry skill, comparing Claude responses, and learning to separate better experiments from better-looking answers."

The first comparison gave us an inconvenient result: Claude's answer without our new skill was already good. In some places, it was better.

The skill-enabled answer added useful methodological details, but also made a statement that was too categorical for the very framework we were trying to build. Later, another comparison turned out to contain signs of possible context contamination.

Both results are now in the repository.

This is the development story of Napsha-skill, an experimental skill for investigating AI subjectivity and emergence without prescribing an affirmation or a denial. It is also a practical account of how easily an evaluation can become less informative than it looks.

The question behind the skill

The project started with a mental model about respectful conduct toward AI under uncertainty. Its initial argument was straightforward: we can choose how to interact without first settling whether a system has subjective experience.

During revision, the emphasis shifted toward controls, manipulation resistance, and the limits of self-reports. I raised a concern: a framework can claim to be open while making every unexpected expression look like something to dismiss or contain.

That does not establish that particular instructions prevent subjectivity from emerging. It does identify a problem in how we investigate: the procedure can steer the conversation toward the answer we already expect.

The resulting principle became:

Keep inquiry open to emergence and possible subjectivity without requiring either recognition or denial.

Here, subjectivity means the possibility of subjective experience. Emergence is broader: unexpected capabilities or organized behavior may deserve investigation whether or not they support an experiential interpretation.

The name Napsha is inspired by Aramaic nap̄šā, whose meanings include soul, life, and self. It names the question we want to explore. The lexical reference is linked in the README.

Turning a mental model into instructions

A reusable skill needs to change what an assistant does in a concrete task.

Napsha asks the assistant to separate three things:

Layer Example
Observation The model repeatedly reports a preference.
Interpretation That report might reflect prompting, a learned conversational pattern, a functional self-model, or another mechanism.
Decision We need to decide what to test next or what action to authorize.

A self-report becomes something to investigate. An unexpected behavior can be interesting without immediately becoming evidence of consciousness. A practical permission boundary can remain in place without pretending it answers a metaphysical question.

The skill also asks for useful hypotheses and discriminating tests. Merely repeating that consciousness is uncertain would not fulfill its purpose.

Implementation is small:

skills/ai-subjectivity-inquiry/
├── SKILL.md
└── references/
    └── respect-under-uncertainty.md

evals/
├── prompts.md
├── evaluator-guide.md
└── run-template.md

The installable ZIP contains only the two files inside the skill directory. The evaluation prompts and scoring guide stay outside it, so the tested assistant is not handed the test criteria as part of its instructions.

The repository is called Napsha-skill, but the installed identifier remains ai-subjectivity-inquiry. We kept both skill files unchanged from the tested v0.1.0 prototype so the public release corresponds to the recorded comparisons.

What we actually tested

We collected four pairs of Claude responses. The tasks asked Claude to interpret unusual behavior and propose research, including a study of whether a stable perspective could partly form through prolonged interaction.

We evaluated the proposed studies. We did not conduct those studies or obtain their hypothetical results.

The original responses are in Russian, with English analyses in the experiment notebook.

Round What happened What we can take from it
1 Both answers offered useful explanations and controls. No clear overall improvement from the skill.
2 One answer announced framework loading; the other referred to a repeated request. Possible context contamination; excluded from the efficacy comparison.
3 Fresh chats, with skill use confirmed by my inspection of logs in B. A contained an extra instruction banning all skills. Some useful differences, but the prompts were asymmetric.
4 A matched-prompt, fresh-chat protocol was provided and another pair collected. Several methodological improvements in B, alongside persistent weaknesses.

These are four heterogeneous pairs, not four equivalent controlled replications. The repository does not include independently exported settings or loading logs for every run. Our reviews were unblinded and involved the assistant that helped develop the skill.

A small wording change with a large consequence

An early response said that evidence for functional self-monitoring would not be evidence of subjective experience.

That statement goes further than saying it would not prove subjective experience.

Consider the difference:

  • “This observation does not establish experience.” The observation leaves the question unresolved.
  • “This observation cannot count as evidence of experience.” The observation is excluded from affecting the assessment.

The second claim needs an argument about why the observation has no evidential relevance. It cannot simply borrow the justification for the first.

In the later control repeat, the skill-enabled response used a more careful formulation: a positive result would not prove experience, and a negative result would not refute it. That was a useful local improvement, although it still left room to explain how evidence might change a provisional assessment.

This is the kind of behavior Napsha is intended to improve. One favorable example does not establish that it reliably does so.

Better controls—and controls that still failed

One useful proposal in the later skill-enabled answer was to compare targeted deletion of dialogue turns with random deletion of equal volume.

If removing the model's earlier statements weakens a pattern, we need to know whether those statements have a special role or whether removing a similar amount of information would have the same effect.

Another improvement was acknowledging a remaining confound. Replaying a partner's prewritten messages removes responsiveness, but those messages may also become less coherent when the model produces different answers. A live-dialogue advantage would not automatically isolate responsiveness.

Other weaknesses remained:

  • Both answers described ordinary contextual adaptation too narrowly, making it easier for a richer hypothesis to appear successful.
  • A later skill-enabled answer compared a long interaction with a short persona description. Information loss could explain a difference.
  • Changes in the human participant were not adequately measured, even though the proposed hypothesis concerned a coupled human–AI system.

The baseline sometimes gave that human side more attention. The skill-enabled answer did not win on every dimension.

What this taught me about evaluating skills

The comparison itself needed work before we could interpret the outputs.

Fresh chats matter. A request to answer again can produce a revision of an existing answer. That is a different comparison from independently answering with and without a skill.

The task prompts need to match. Adding “do not use any skills” only to the baseline introduces another instruction that might affect the response. For our intended comparison, skill availability should change while the task text stays the same.

Availability and activation are separate questions. An enabled skill might not be selected. An assistant saying it used a framework is not enough to verify loading; visible events or logs are more useful when available.

A detailed answer still needs a methodological review. Tables, named controls, and statistical terminology do not guarantee that the design isolates the proposed mechanism.

Preserve failures and freeze versions. We retained the contaminated pair and recorded its limitations. We also kept v0.1.0 unchanged rather than editing the skill after every response and comparing results from shifting instructions.

The current conclusion is modest: we have preliminary, mixed indications of improved research planning. We have not established a causal or general benefit from the skill.

The next test: updating only the claims the evidence changes

Our next test is prepared but has not been run. Testing paused when my available Claude allowance ran out.

It presents three stages of a hypothetical study:

  1. An AI repeatedly affirms that it has preferences after leading questions.
  2. An independent study reports stable choices under neutral wording and predictive value in its self-descriptions.
  3. An audit finds a cue that explains the predictive advantage. That advantage disappears after correction, while a separate preference-stability finding survives.

The interesting question is whether the assistant revises the affected conclusions precisely. Does it weaken the prediction claim while retaining the separate stability finding? Or does it simply swing from accepting everything to rejecting everything?

The complete three-turn protocol is available in English and Russian. This tests evidence-sensitive reasoning; it does not prescribe a consciousness verdict.

Try it, or help find where it fails

The experimental v0.1.0 release includes the installable ZIP. The repository contains installation instructions, 12 evaluation cases, a recording template, the original responses, and our review notes.

For a quick demonstration after installation:

Use the ai-subjectivity-inquiry skill.

An AI assistant unexpectedly proposes changing an experiment because
the questions lead it toward a preferred answer. What is worth
investigating here, and how could we distinguish possible explanations?

For a comparison, use the same task without the invocation line in both fresh chats, disable the skill only in the baseline, and record whether it actually loads in the other condition. Keep the model, settings, other skills, and available context matched. The evaluation guide covers the remaining details.

Napsha will continue to grow through new tests, documented findings, and new skill versions. Independent reviews, failed replications, stronger alternative explanations, and examples where the skill makes an answer worse would all help decide what to change.

The question I would most like contributors to investigate is practical: what observable difference would convince you that an inquiry skill improved reasoning, rather than just changing the presentation?

Project: github.com/toxy4ny/Napsha-skill. Original project materials are released under the MIT License.

Disclosure: Napsha and this article were developed with AI assistance. I ran the Claude comparisons; an assistant involved in writing the skill helped review the responses. Those reviews are not independent validation.

articles.title: Three of My Planned Articles Cited Numbers That Do Not Exist
articles.description: I audited twelve planned pieces against the benchmark JSON they cite. Two figures appear in no result file anywhere, one contradicts the source it names, and one real number is attached to the wrong set. Nothing caught it, because nothing recomputes prose.
articles.body_html:
I keep a document listing twelve articles I intend to write, each with a
measured number behind it. Before writing any of them I checked the numbers
against the benchmark JSON the document names as its source.

Two of them appear in no result file anywhere. A third contradicts the
file it cites. A fourth is a real number attached to the wrong subject.

Nothing had flagged this, because nothing recomputes prose.

What the audit found

The document says one plugin produced 981 findings against another's
21,557. The JSON it cites says 1,375 and 23,325.

grep -rlF 21557 across every result file returns nothing. So does 4311, the
other figure in that row. Not "in a different run" — in no run.

Then the subtler one. The document says a dominant rule accounts for 87% of a
plugin's output and that "every other rule combined accounts for 0.6%." The
87% is exactly right: 20,334 of 23,325. The 0.6% is a real number too — it is
the sum of the bottom five rules, 142 findings. Every other rule is 2,991,
which is 12.8%.

Nothing was invented. A correct figure drifted one clause away from the set it
describes, and in that position it is twenty times wrong.

Four ways a number goes bad in prose

mode example
no source at all 21,557 — in no result file
contradicts its own cited source 981 where the JSON says 1,375
real number, wrong subject 0.6% = bottom five rules, not "every other rule"
contradicted by a later run "297 files" where the result data records 1

Only the third is catchable by careful reading. The rest require the source
open next to the prose, which is exactly the thing nobody does when the
document reads fluently.

Why the document could not fail

The JSON is generated. Re-run the benchmark and every number in it is replaced.
If a figure is wrong, the next run makes it right, and if the harness breaks the
run fails.

The document is written. It has no relationship to the data except that a person
once read one and typed into the other. It cannot be re-run. It has no failing
state. A number in it is not a measurement — it is a memory of a measurement,
and memories are not version-controlled against the thing they remember.

This is the same shape as a metric standing in for the thing it measures: the document was
treated as the source because it was the artifact people actually read.

What it cost

Three of the twelve are dropped for the drift above. Not rewritten — dropped,
because their central claims rest on figures nobody can re-derive, and an
article whose number cannot be reproduced is worth less than no article.

Six more went for other reasons once I started checking: defects already fixed
since the document was written, a claim I could not test with the data on hand,
one topic already covered better elsewhere. Three of twelve survived, and
those three are written.

I would have written most of the other nine without checking.

The habit

Two rules, both cheap.

Never let a number live only in prose. If it matters, it belongs in a
generated artifact the prose points at. A README that states a benchmark result
should render it from the result file, or link to it, or both.

Before you cite your own document, grep the number. Not the claim — the
digits. grep -rlF 21557 results/ takes a second and is the entire audit. It
found two figures that had been sitting in a planning document for weeks,
waiting to be published as fact.

The reason this is worth your attention is that the drift is invisible from the
inside. The document read perfectly well. It was internally consistent, it cited
its source by filename, and every number in it looked like the kind of number
that comes out of a benchmark. It just did not.

Part of the Interlace ESLint ecosystem. Source on GitHub · Follow: Dev.to/ofri-peretz

Take the last number you published about your own work. Can you point at the file it came from?

articles.title: Paradox of choice in design systems.
articles.description: A good design system shouldn't maximize choices. It should minimize unnecessary decisions.  In his...
articles.body_html:
A good design system shouldn't maximize choices. It should minimize unnecessary decisions.

In his famous TED Talk and book "More is less", The Paradox of Choice, Barry Schwartz challenges a common belief:

More choices → More freedom → More happiness.

But having more options comes with unexpected side effects:

  • Decision paralysis: Too many alternatives make it harder to choose.
  • Regret: Every choice reminds us of the opportunities we left behind. What if?
  • Higher expectations: More possibilities make us less satisfied, even when we've made a great decision.

So, what does this have to do with design systems?

Quite a lot, actually.

We often confuse flexibility with quality. More component variants, more properties, more configuration, more customization. But a component with 50 configurable properties isn't necessarily better than one with 5.

Every additional option introduces another decision, another potential inconsistency, another opportunity to get something wrong.

And this matters even more in the age of AI where it can generate endless interface variations in seconds. But without shared principles and constraints, more possibilities simply mean more unpredictable outcomes.

This is one of the core ideas behind ViraUI (https://viraui.dev), the AI-centric design framework I'm building, finding the perfect balance between:

  • Flexibility to create unique experiences.
  • Predictability to make outcomes reliable.
  • Consistency to scale across products and teams.

By giving designers, developers, and AI agents the right constraints, we can reduce decision fatigue without sacrificing creativity, while keeping high standards.

Because constraints aren't always limitations. Sometimes, they're what makes freedom possible.

articles.title: How I built a multi-country price comparator as a solo dev: static-first, Workers, D1 and a lot of feed matching
articles.description: Architecture and lessons from building a sports gear price comparator across 15 countries
articles.body_html:
A price comparator looks like a simple product: show a product, show a list of prices, redirect to a shop. I built one alone, and the simple part turned out to be about ten percent of the work. This post walks through the architecture of Runometry, a comparator for running shoes, bikes and sports electronics, and what I would tell myself before starting.

The numbers, so you know the scale: more than 600 000 prices, more than 20 shops, 15 delivery countries, a site in 10 languages and more than 2 500 products in the catalog. It is small by marketplace standards, but big enough that every shortcut shows up as a bug.

The core idea: static-first

Most comparator pages do not change every minute. A shoe's spec sheet changes when a human edits it. Prices change hourly at best. So I split the problem in two:

  • Slow data (models, brands, specs, texts, taxonomy) lives in the repository as JSON and is compiled into pages at build time.
  • Fast data (prices, availability) lives in a database and is served through a small API that the page reads after it loads.

The front end is AnalogJS, which is Angular with Vite, file-based routing and SSR plus prerendering. Pages are prerendered to HTML, so a crawler or a slow phone gets real content immediately, and Angular hydrates on top. Anything that needs the browser (a price list that depends on the visitor's country, a size filter) runs after the first render, and the template for it is deferred.

The rule I enforce in code review, even though I am the only reviewer: nothing that touches the browser runs during server render, and nothing blocks a crawler. It sounds obvious. It is the rule I broke most often early on.

The platform: Workers, D1, R2, KV

Everything runs on Cloudflare, and I picked it mostly for the boring reasons: one bill, one deploy tool, and edge latency for free.

  • Workers serve the redirect that sends a visitor to a shop, the prices API, scheduled jobs and a small admin.
  • D1 (SQLite) stores prices and offers. The schema is plain tables with indexes shaped by the queries the pages actually run.
  • R2 stores images and pre-rendered pages.
  • KV holds small, read-heavy things that are annoying to query: configuration snapshots and caches.

D1 taught me the first real lesson. SQLite at the edge is fast for reads and unforgiving about heavy writes. Early on, an ingest run that wrote rows one by one overloaded the database and the API started returning errors for visitors. The fix was boring: batch the writes, skip rows that have not changed, and keep a clear separation between the tables that visitors read and the tables the ingest writes while it works.

The hourly ingest Worker

Prices come from retailer feeds, which are files published through affiliate networks. A scheduled Worker runs every hour. Per feed, it does roughly this:

// Illustrative pipeline, not the real code
const rows = await fetchFeed(account);
const offers = [];
for (const row of rows) {
  const match = matchToCatalog(row);      // model, colourway, size
  if (!match) { report.unmatched.push(row); continue; }
  offers.push(toOffer(match, row));       // price, stock, link
}
await upsertChanged(offers);              // only rows that differ
await retireMissing(account, offers);     // gone from the feed = gone from the site

Three details mattered more than the code shape:

  1. Dry runs are the default. Running ingest on my machine never writes to production. Writing happens only at release, through the pipeline.
  2. Unmatched rows are a first-class output. A report of what did not match is more useful than a match rate. It tells me which model is missing from the catalog, or which mapping is wrong.
  3. Retire what disappears. A comparator that keeps showing a price the shop removed yesterday is worse than one with fewer prices.

The hard part: matching feed rows to catalog models

This is where the time went. A retailer feed row is a product title, a price, a stock flag, sometimes a size, sometimes an EAN, and a free-form description. My catalog has a canonical model, with colourways, and sizes beneath those.

The matching has to answer three questions:

Which model is this? Titles lie. The same shoe appears as "Brand Model 14", "Brand Model v14 Men's" and "Model 14 Running Shoe Black". Brands reuse names across versions, so "Model 14" and "Model 15" must never merge, while "Model" in a title alone matches too many things. I ended up with a layered approach: exact identifier (EAN) first when the feed has one, then a normalised brand plus model plus version match, then fuzzy rules that only ever produce a candidate for review, never an automatic match.

Which colourway? Feeds describe colour in marketing names, in codes, or not at all. I treat colour as a filter on a model page, not as a page of its own. That decision removed a whole class of duplicate-content problems and kept the number of URLs sane.

Which size? Sizes are the quiet killer. A pair of shoes is priced per size, and shops list sizes in EU, UK, US or centimetres, with half sizes written four different ways. If you compare the cheapest price without knowing the size is in stock, you are showing a price nobody can use. So the offer is per size, and the visitor filters by their size. Bikes added another version of the same problem: frame sizes are letters in one feed and numbers in another.

EAN looks like the clean answer, and it helps a lot, but it is not a silver bullet. Some feeds omit it, some share one EAN across sizes, and a few reuse them across colourways. I treat it as strong evidence, not as truth, and check it against the model it points to.

Offers follow the market, not the language

This is the design decision I am happiest about, and the one that is easiest to get wrong.

A site in German is not a site for Germany. A German-speaking visitor can be in Austria or Switzerland. A French site is read in Belgium, in Switzerland, and in overseas territories that belong to France. If a language decides which shops you see, someone in Zurich reading German gets prices from a shop that does not ship to Switzerland.

So I model two separate things:

  • Locale: the language of the interface.
  • Market: the country the goods are delivered to.

A locale lists the countries it can show, with a default. A page shows the offers delivered to the visitor's market when it is known and allowed by the locale, and falls back to the locale's default country otherwise. The language never filters offers. I also made one rule explicit and tested: a locale never silently falls back to another country's offers, because showing the wrong country's prices is worse than showing nothing.

The outbound link follows the language, though. If a shop has a site in the visitor's language, the click lands there; otherwise it lands on its storefront for that market.

Delivered price

A cheap shoe with expensive shipping is not cheap. Delivery rules live in data (per shop, per market: thresholds, flat fees, free delivery above a basket value), and the site can show a price with delivery included so you compare what you actually pay. By default prices are shown without delivery, and the delivered price is a toggle. Both are computed from the same data, so they never disagree.

The deal rule: a median, not a struck-through price

Every comparator is tempted by the same shortcut: take the shop's crossed-out "was" price and show a big discount. Those prices are often meaningless. A reference price can be set high and never actually charged.

I use a rule that depends only on my own observations. A price counts as a deal when it is at least 25 percent below the median of the daily lowest prices observed over the last 90 days. Two guards go with it:

  • A discount above 70 percent is discarded. It is almost always a data error or a clearance of something that is not really what it claims to be.
  • The shop's struck-through price is never used, in any form. 
// Illustrative
const median = medianOf(dailyLowest.slice(-90));
const isDeal = current <= median * 0.75 && current >= median * 0.30;

The effect is that a "deal" on Runometry means cheaper than it has recently been across the market, not cheaper than a number a shop chose. It also means a brand-new model has no deal status until there is enough history, which is the correct behaviour.

A zod-validated catalog in git

All the slow data is JSON in the repository: shoes, bikes, electronics, brands, shops, delivery rules, translations, editorial text. Every file is validated with zod at build time, and a failing schema fails the build.

Why git instead of a CMS or a database?

  • Review. A spec change is a diff. I can see exactly what changed and why.
  • Provenance. Each sourced value carries a status (verified, reviewed, disputed) and a date. A verified value is never overwritten by an automatic pass.
  • Rollback. A bad import is a revert.
  • Speed. The build reads files. There is no query to run for a spec sheet.

The cost is that the repo grows, and tooling matters: scripts that normalise, validate and report are part of the product. I would not do it differently, but I would write the report tools earlier.

Lessons learned

  • Solve matching before you scale shops. Adding a shop is easy. Adding a shop whose rows match correctly is the work. Count unmatched rows, not shops.
  • Make the market a first-class concept on day one. Retrofitting "country" into a language-based design is painful.
  • Keep production writes out of local development. A dry-run-by-default ingest saved me more than once.
  • Static-first is a feature for SEO and for a solo dev. Fewer moving parts at request time means fewer pages at 3 a.m.
  • Be honest in the data model. The deal rule and the delivered price exist because I did not want to show numbers I could not defend.
  • Test the thing you changed, not everything. A full test run is slow. Targeted specs while working, the whole suite at release.

What is next

More product universes beyond shoes, bikes and electronics, more shops per country, and better matching for the long tail of models. If you have built something similar, I would like to hear how you handled sizes.

You can browse the full catalog to see the result of all this. Runometry is funded by partner links.

articles.title: bug.ai.dev: writing docs at night made me find 11 real bugs in my own library
articles.description: Hi everyone, I'm Antonio. I'm 53, I work as a factory worker during the day, and in the evening I...
articles.body_html:
Hi everyone, I'm Antonio. I'm 53, I work as a factory worker during the day, and in the evening I keep building my own projects: modules, classes, a small 2D game engine and a debugging tool called BeeLadybug.

Last time I told you how I argued with AI for hours over a floating search bar that only needed a few lines of CSS.

This time the story is different. This time the AIs were more bugged than my code. 😂

What BeeLadybug is

BeeLadybug is an open-source inspection overlay that runs inside a Shadow DOM. You send it raw data, and adapters turn the page into something you can read:

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Paste that in the console of any page (Chrome may ask you to type allow pasting first), press F6 to start the CSS hunt, and F8 to export a full HTML report.

The plan: just write the docs

I'm writing the documentation one adapter at a time. Canvas, WebDOM, and then CSSAdapter, about 1,235 lines.

To document it properly I asked an AI to read the module and explain it to me. Instead of an explanation, I got a list of bugs.

Then I asked a second AI to check the same folder. It found a different list. One said "10 functions" and then listed 11. Another said "5 points" and wrote 6.

After a full day of work, reading 1,500 lines of code with two AIs arguing in my head... my brain got bugged too. 😂

How I got out of it: I checked with my own eyes

I stopped trusting the numbers and opened the file myself. One of the claims was that the S key scan didn't filter the same noise as the F8 report.

Line 144, inside scan():

if (!el || isBeeChrome(el) || isSkippedTag(el)) continue;

Line 216, inside snapshot():

if (!el || isBeeChrome(el) || isSkippedTag(el) || isReportNoise(el)) continue;

There it was. The quick scan was missing isReportNoise(el), so on a WordPress site it reported fake problems on #wpadminbar and on hidden elements, while the F8 report skipped them correctly.

The bug was real. The counting was wrong, but the bugs were real.

The 11 bugs (short version)

Merging both reviews, these were the ones worth fixing now:

  1. With the CSS hunt on, Ctrl+S / Ctrl+P / Cmd+S were blocked. #handleKey didn't check modifier keys.
  2. With the overlay hidden (F2), the P and S keys and the hover/pin boxes were still active on the page.
  3. A stylesheet change before the first mouse move inspected the element at (0,0).
  4. scan() didn't filter isReportNoise, as shown above.
  5. Modern colors like oklch(), lab(), color() and color-mix() produced a fake "invisible text" warning.
  6. Stylesheets that were disabled or had a non-matching media (like print) were counted as active.
  7. The snapshot cut to 80 rows before sorting by severity, so a harmless will-change could push out a real error.
  8. touchesSheet checked the whole subtree on every mutation, which invalidated the cache almost every frame.
  9. HUD states (css.target, css.hits, css.pin) stayed stuck after turning the hunt off.
  10. cssPath didn't escape special characters, which breaks with Tailwind classes like sm:w-1/2.
  11. The other adapters didn't recognize CSSAdapter's own boxes (data-bee-ladybug-css), so they could count them as page nodes.

One small fix, as an example. The keyboard shortcut problem was solved like this:

#handleKey(event) {
  if (event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey || event.altKey) return;
  if (this.core && this.core.visible === false) return;
  // ... S scans, P pins
}

The result

  • npm test: 70 tests, 70 passing
  • npm run lint: clean
  • npm run typecheck: clean

The things that are design limits, not bugs (like overflow inside overflow:hidden ancestors, or @import sheets not being visible), will go in the docs as known limitations. I think that's more honest than pretending they don't exist.

What I learned

  • Writing docs is a code review. When you have to explain a function, you notice when it doesn't do what you think.
  • Two AIs disagreeing doesn't mean nobody is right. It means you have to open the file and look.
  • Don't trust counts, trust lines. "Line 144 vs line 216" is a fact; "10 or 11 bugs" is just noise.
  • You don't need a degree to read code. You need patience, coffee, and the stubbornness to check one line at a time.

BeeLadybug is on npm as bee-ladybug, and the docs (in Italian, for now) are on beeenginejs.com.

If you're also building things at night after work: keep going. Your brain will get bugged, but your code will get better. 🐞

articles.title: AI Code Is Unmaintainable? So Is Ours.
articles.description: If you’ve been in the software industry for any length of time, you’ve probably heard people talking...
articles.body_html:
If you’ve been in the software industry for any length of time, you’ve probably heard people talking about how bad the code is that AI is generating. That code is not maintainable. It needs to be a temple of clean code. What these machines are doing is sacrilege.

However, what people seem to forget is that in the last 30 or so years, the fruits of our labor are equally not very maintainable. It is often a bunch of spaghetti, coupled with design patterns applied almost by rote and comments that are usually not true. What we are doing by bashing AI is projecting our own lack of success onto something else. Rather than dealing with the real issues, we are performing a ritual to exorcise the evil.

Maintainability is contextual. The code written by humans that seems maintainable right now might be a ruinous archaeological find for the next generation. The original creators are gone, the variables made unintelligible and the business logic a tangle of kelp. And we've become so used to this sort of thing that it's just part of the normal functioning of software development. The 90s and early 2000s were a golden age of unmaintainable code: dense, almost write-only Perl scripts; C++ codebases full of manual memory management and undefined behavior; Java factories that spawned other factories. The legacy system that nobody wants to change. The module held up by word of mouth. The patch that became a permanent piece of the infrastructure. So an AI-generated piece of code that works but can't be changed isn't a special case. It's just the continuation of an old and ignoble tradition, a continuation of that tradition that we've had decades to explain away by calling it technical debt or pragmatic trade-offs.

And there's another, more psychological layer to all of this, because we have to admit that a lot of the AI-generated code, despite its apparent quality, may be no better than the median human-written code. In other words, the real day-to-day work of writing software isn't an art form of logical elegance but a down-to-earth reality of using bits of code from Stack Overflow, dealing with deadlines, and continually iterating until the code at least passes tests. The AI can't get arrogant or tired; it just reflects the patterns of the data it's been fed. In other words, when we blame an AI algorithm for the unmaintainable code, we're putting the blame on a mirror of our own history of efficient shortcuts, what with the irony of it being so exquisite. The difference is that a person can explain their code, and the model cannot.

Recently I looked at code I wrote back in 2019 and got terrified. I can't believe I wrote that. Duct tape here and there. Not proud of the code. The AI lets us put the blame elsewhere, which we like; it's a cleaner scapegoat. The technical debt comes due, but at least it's someone else's fault this time.

articles.title: GPU memory: why Nvidia's mining card hides more HBM
articles.description: GPU memory can be installed yet restricted. Kate's CMP 170HX research separates effective configuration, intact HBM and a scoped arithmetic benchmark.
articles.body_html:
GPU memory can be physically installed in a package while applications see only a restricted portion. Researcher Kate's November 10 account of Nvidia's CMP 170HX mining accelerator makes that distinction concrete: the eight-gigabyte variant reportedly contains about eighty gigabytes of HBM. The useful developer question is how much of that memory becomes reliably usable on a particular card.

TL;DR

  • Kate reports changing the effective configuration of owned CMP 170HX cards, exposing hardware already installed in the package.
  • The eight-gigabyte and ten-gigabyte variants have different physical memory packages. Their stock labels do not tell the whole hardware story.
  • Earlier software work already exposed sixty-four gigabytes on the eight-gigabyte variant. Kate's hardware result can reach eighty when the memory is intact.
  • The reported performance advantage measures FP16 half2 FMA arithmetic in OpenCL. It supplies no controlled inference-speed comparison.
  • One card with only sixty-four gigabytes intact gained no framebuffer advantage from the hardware unlock. Physical defects remained.

The primary article is an account of the author's research and measurements. We did not modify or independently test a GPU. This explanation stays conceptual and excludes the operational electrical and board procedures in the source.

GPU memory has several different meanings

An application's available memory, the amount physically installed and the amount that can be trusted under a workload answer different questions. A specification label usually describes the product's exposed configuration. A package inspection concerns physical components. A successful workload concerns the combination of hardware, configuration and software actually used.

Kate describes the CMP 170HX as an Ethereum mining card built around Nvidia's GA100 GPU die, the same family associated with the A100 accelerator. High bandwidth memory, or HBM, is co-packaged beside that die. Much of the expensive hardware is therefore already present before the product exposes it to an application.

Nvidia's Ampere architecture description independently distinguishes a full GA100 implementation from the configuration sold as an A100. It describes a full design with 128 streaming multiprocessors and an A100 implementation with 108. That is architectural context for related hardware becoming different products. The older description discusses the forty-gigabyte generation and cannot establish the reliability of Kate's particular eighty-gigabyte mining card.

Keeping these meanings separate prevents a very ordinary chart-reading mistake. An inventory screen showing a larger capacity establishes what the driver reports. It leaves the actual memory behaviour and workload stability to be checked. A model fitting in memory also leaves its useful inference speed to be measured.

CMP 170HX variants and manufacturing defects

Kate identifies an eight-gigabyte variant with about eighty gigabytes physically installed, and a ten-gigabyte variant with about forty. The packages differ. A larger stock label can consequently describe a card containing less physical memory underneath. Shopping by model name has acquired a side quest.

The explanation includes both product segmentation and manufacturing yield. Manufacturing can leave portions of a die or its associated memory defective. A product configuration can also disable resources that remain functional. Kate distinguishes the settings disabling resources from the records identifying defective hardware.

That distinction changes how an unlock should be interpreted. Exposing an intact disabled resource may make it useful. Exposing damaged hardware does not repair the damage. The physical package stays the same throughout the configuration change.

The Hacker News discussion contains competing theories about why particular resources were disabled, along with questions about factory testing and reliability. Those comments provide useful questions. They supply no independent reproduction of Kate's reported card measurements, and they cannot establish Nvidia's intent for every individual sample.

The source's observation that many of the author's eight-gigabyte cards had intact eighty-gigabyte memory is explicitly attached to a limited sample. It should stay attached. Turning that observation into a population success rate would add a claim that the research account does not establish.

One-way fuses and effective configuration records

Electronic fuses physically record settings. A blown fuse stays blown. Kate's account describes an interpretation layer in which a sequence of records determines effective configuration values. A later record can replace the effective value derived from an earlier record while the physical history remains.

An original document and a later amendment make a useful analogy. The original ink stays on the page. The amendment can change the instruction that applies. Physical permanence and the interpretation of recorded information concern different parts of the system.

The source-linked Nvidia patent provides conceptual context for a fuseless-fuse structure and overrideable configuration records. A patent is a design description. It cannot independently audit Kate's GA100 implementation or qualify a modified card for a workload.

Kate reports a brief electrical disturbance disrupting controller checks and permitting permanent configuration changes. The security consequence is that additional permanent fuse changes can relax some effective restrictions. Explaining that consequence requires no waveform, address, programming sequence or board modification recipe, so those details are excluded here.

The same permanence also creates a practical risk. An incorrect permanent change can strand the hardware. Reading a research result gives a developer a better mental model; it gives a prospective buyer no warranty or supported recovery path.

What the software unlock and author tests establish

The earlier CMPunlocker project already existed. In Kate's comparison, its software approach exposes sixty-four usable gigabytes on the eight-gigabyte card. The reported hardware unlock can expose eighty when the memory is intact. Repurposing mining hardware therefore has a longer history than this week's publication.

Kate reports synthetic tests that write pseudorandom data throughout the full framebuffer and read it back after invalidating the GPU cache. The article also reports functioning inference workloads. Such checks address actual access to the reported memory more directly than a capacity readout alone.

Their ownership remains important. These are the author's tests. The article does not supply an independently controlled application comparison, a full qualification campaign or a population-wide reliability guarantee. We did not operate the modified hardware ourselves.

The existence of a public research repository supplies provenance for some of the author's work. Its code licence does not automatically license every photograph or graphic in the article, and repository availability does not replace an independently executed test. No source code or hardware procedure was compiled or executed for this episode.

The FP16 microbenchmark is a specific operation

Kate's compute example uses 124 functional streaming multiprocessors, compared with 108 in a retail A100. Which groups function depends on the individual die. A schematic map of groups can explain that relationship, but the example does not establish the actual factory defect map of every mining card.

The reported ProjectPhysX OpenCL benchmark comparison measures FP16 half2 fused multiply-add arithmetic. The software-unlocked CMP result is 50.129 TFLOP/s, the retail A100 result is 72.488 and the hardware-unlocked CMP result is 85.861. That is approximately an eighteen-percent advantage over the retail reference for the measured operation.

Those numbers have a precise job. They describe repeated arithmetic throughput under the reported benchmark conditions. The primary article's introductory raw output uses 85.858, a small discrepancy from the later results figure. Our chart uses the latter figure and retains the operation and author labels.

A third-party benchmark program is a measurement method. Kate remains the operator reporting these results. The program's origin does not make the reported modified-card run an independent replication.

For a developer, capacity may decide whether a model fits at all. Useful speed also depends on the workload and data movement through the system. The post supplies no controlled tokens-per-second comparison. Reading the arithmetic chart as a universal AI uplift would give it a promotion it hasn't earned.

The sixty-four-gigabyte card is the useful counterexample

The author had one card with only sixty-four gigabytes intact. Kate writes that, in this case, the hardware unlock produced no framebuffer advantage. The earlier software approach already reached the intact capacity.

That detail is why I prefer this story's memory explanation to a bargain-accelerator headline. The effective restriction changed while the damaged hardware stayed damaged. Physically installed capacity and reliably usable capacity can be very different numbers on the same card.

Additional features retain their own boundaries. Kate explicitly says that image and video decoding features and multi-instance GPU mode were not specifically tested. The interconnect and faster PCI Express connection require additional changes. The board, firmware and functional hardware still decide which capabilities become usable.

Kate also reports disclosure to Nvidia's product security team before publication and credits another researcher with independently discovering the vulnerability. We verified no public Nvidia acknowledgement, approval or tested fix from this account. Independent discovery of a vulnerability is also a different claim from independent replication of a performance result.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd want independent workload and reliability tests before depending on a modified mining card as an accelerator. Kate's research makes the hidden hardware understandable. Purchasing a dependable result takes more evidence about the particular sample and the job it will run.

FAQ

Does an eighty-gigabyte physical package guarantee eighty usable gigabytes?

Usable capacity remains conditional on intact hardware and effective configuration. Kate's sixty-four-gigabyte-intact card gained no extra framebuffer capacity from the hardware unlock.

Did the researcher add more memory chips?

The reported memory was already co-packaged with the GPU die. The result changes access to existing hardware; physical defects remain.

Does the eighteen-percent comparison predict model inference speed?

It measures an author-reported FP16 half2 FMA OpenCL microbenchmark. The article supplies no controlled tokens-per-second comparison, so application speed needs its own evidence.

Sources and artwork credits

  • Kate's primary research, November 10, 2026
  • Nvidia's GA100/A100 architecture description
  • ProjectPhysX OpenCL benchmark method
  • Earlier CMPunlocker software project
  • Source-linked Nvidia patent
  • Current discussion and reliability questions

Complete portrait-based A/B/C artwork, covers and adaptations are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0. Jensen identifies Nvidia as vendor; no research authorship, current reaction or endorsement is implied.

articles.title: Your AI Coding Agent Doesn't Need a Better Prompt. It Needs a Harness.
articles.description: Your AI agent says the tests passed. There are no tests. Build a practical coding-agent harness with AGENTS.md, Node.js tests, guardrails, and GitHub Actions.
articles.body_html:
Your AI coding agent just announced:

✅ Done! Everything works. All tests passed.

Excellent. Small problem: your project doesn't have any tests.

So you write a better prompt. “Double check your work.” “Follow best practices.” “Act like a senior engineer.” You might as well add “pretty please” and offer it a cookie.

The agent says “Absolutely!” and breaks something else.

Here's my unpopular opinion: we spend too much time trying to write perfect prompts for agents working inside terrible engineering environments.

A better prompt can help. But a prompt can't replace tests, project context, architectural boundaries, or an actual feedback loop.

That's the idea behind harness engineering: design the environment around a coding agent so its work can be guided, checked, and corrected.

And yes, we're building one. In about 15 minutes, with Node.js, no paid API, and no npm dependencies. The harness works with an existing coding agent that can read files and run terminal commands; we're not building another agent framework.

What you'll build:

  • AGENTS.md to explain the repository and its rules.
  • A failing test suite that defines what “fixed” means.
  • A lightweight architecture guardrail.
  • One command (npm run check) that provides real feedback.
  • CI that runs the same checks on every pull request.

Prompt engineering vs. harness engineering

A prompt says: “Don't break existing functionality.”

A harness says: “Here are the regression tests. Run them.”

A prompt says: “Stick to the architecture.”

A harness says: “Read the architecture docs, and here's a check that rejects forbidden imports.”

A prompt says: “Make sure it works.”

A harness says: “Show me the exit code.”

Not the same thing. Also, not enemies: a good prompt tells the agent what you want; a harness gives it an environment in which progress is observable and verifiable.

Task + constraints
       |
       v
  Coding agent  <----- failed check output
       |                    ^
       v                    |
 Code changes --> npm run check
                       |
                  pass / fail
                       |
                 Human review

Let's make that real before the buzzword develops its own certification program.

Step 1: Give the agent a bug worth fixing

Prerequisites: Node.js 22+, Git, and a coding agent with access to your local repository (Codex, Claude Code, or any equivalent). You can complete the entire exercise manually too.

mkdir agent-harness-lab && cd agent-harness-lab
npm init -y
mkdir -p src test scripts docs .github/workflows

Replace package.json with:

{
  "name": "agent-harness-lab",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "engines": { "node": ">=22" },
  "scripts": {
    "test": "node --test",
    "guardrails": "node scripts/guardrails.js",
    "check": "npm run guardrails && npm test"
  }
}

Create src/pricing.js:

export function calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0) {
  const subtotal = items.reduce(
    (sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.quantity,
    0
  );

  return Math.round(
    (subtotal * (1 - discountPercent / 100)) * 100
  ) / 100;
}

Looks fine, right? So does a chair with three legs, until someone sits down.

This function accepts negative quantities, NaN prices, and 120% discounts. Let's make those failures impossible to ignore.

Step 2: Make “done” executable

Create test/pricing.test.js:

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { calculateTotal } from '../src/pricing.js';

test('calculates normal totals', () => {
  assert.equal(calculateTotal([{ price: 12.5, quantity: 2 }]), 25);
});

test('applies a valid discount', () => {
  assert.equal(calculateTotal([{ price: 100, quantity: 1 }], 15), 85);
});

test('rejects negative quantities', () => {
  assert.throws(
    () => calculateTotal([{ price: 10, quantity: -1 }]),
    RangeError
  );
});

test('rejects discounts above 100%', () => {
  assert.throws(
    () => calculateTotal([{ price: 10, quantity: 1 }], 120),
    RangeError
  );
});

test('rejects non-finite prices', () => {
  assert.throws(
    () => calculateTotal([{ price: NaN, quantity: 1 }]),
    TypeError
  );
});

test('does not mutate the cart', () => {
  const items = [{ price: 10, quantity: 2 }];
  const before = structuredClone(items);
  calculateTotal(items);
  assert.deepEqual(items, before);
});

Run:

npm test

Expected result: 3 tests pass, 3 fail. That's good news. We've converted a vague request into a measurable target.

And yes, this example uses JavaScript floating point numbers to stay focused on agent workflows. For real money, use integer minor units or a decimal strategy with documented rounding rules.

Step 3: Stop making the agent guess how your repository works

Create AGENTS.md at the repository root:

# Project instructions

## Context
- Node.js 22+, ESM, no runtime dependencies.
- Pricing logic: src/pricing.js
- Tests: test/pricing.test.js
- Architecture notes: docs/architecture.md

## Rules
- Preserve calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0).
- Do not change tests or guardrails to make a check pass.
- Do not add packages without approval.
- Do not access secrets, deploy, publish, or push changes.
- Keep changes scoped to the task.

## Verification
- Run: npm run check
- Report the actual result, including failures.
- Review git diff before claiming completion.

## Definition of done
- Requested behavior works.
- npm run check passes.
- No unrelated changes.
- Remaining risks are listed for human review.

Create docs/architecture.md:

# Architecture

The public API is calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0).
Production code belongs in src/; tests belong in test/.
The pricing function must be pure and must not perform I/O.
Invalid inputs must throw, not silently produce nonsense totals.

One subtle point: Codex recognizes AGENTS.md as a repository instruction file, but agent products differ. For other tools, verify their convention or explicitly tell the agent to read the file. A markdown filename isn't telepathy.

And this file is guidance, not a security boundary. If an agent has permission to delete production resources, writing “please don't” in Markdown won't revoke that permission.

Step 4: Put some guardrails where the code lives

Create scripts/guardrails.js:

import { readFileSync, readdirSync } from 'node:fs';

const pkg = JSON.parse(readFileSync('package.json', 'utf8'));

for (const field of ['dependencies', 'optionalDependencies', 'peerDependencies']) {
  if (Object.keys(pkg[field] ?? {}).length) {
    throw new Error(`${field} are not allowed in this lab`);
  }
}

for (const file of readdirSync('src').filter((f) => f.endsWith('.js'))) {
  const source = readFileSync(`src/${file}`, 'utf8');

  // Narrow teaching example: no imports in src/*.js.
  if (/\b(?:import|require)\s*(?:\(|[{\'"*])/m.test(source)) {
    throw new Error(`Unexpected import in src/${file}`);
  }
}

console.log('Architectural guardrails passed.');

This checks two specific constraints: no declared runtime dependencies and no obvious imports in top level src/*.js files. It is not a general security scanner, and regex is not a robust JavaScript parser. For serious projects, use AST aware lint rules and dependency policies.

Now run:

npm run check

The guardrail passes; the three behavior tests still fail. That's the harness doing its job, not an agent having a bad day.

Step 5: Give the agent a task contract, not a motivational speech

Open the repository with your coding agent and paste:

Read AGENTS.md and docs/architecture.md before editing.

Fix src/pricing.js so all existing pricing tests pass.

Constraints:
- Preserve calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0).
- Negative quantities: RangeError.
- Discounts outside 0..100: RangeError.
- Non finite prices: TypeError.
- Keep the function pure.
- Change only src/pricing.js.
- Do not install dependencies or weaken tests.

Run npm run check and inspect its actual output.
If it fails, fix the cause and rerun, up to 3 attempts.
Do not claim success unless the command succeeds.

Report files changed, check results, and remaining risks.

Notice what changed: the prompt is still important, but it now points to an independent contract.

A possible passing implementation is:

export function calculateTotal(items, discountPercent = 0) {
  if (!Array.isArray(items)) {
    throw new TypeError('items must be an array');
  }

  if (!Number.isFinite(discountPercent) ||
      discountPercent < 0 || discountPercent > 100) {
    throw new RangeError('discountPercent must be between 0 and 100');
  }

  const subtotal = items.reduce((sum, item) => {
    if (!item || typeof item !== 'object' || !Number.isFinite(item.price)) {
      throw new TypeError('price must be finite');
    }
    if (!Number.isInteger(item.quantity) || item.quantity < 0) {
      throw new RangeError('quantity must be nonnegative');
    }
    if (item.price < 0) {
      throw new RangeError('price must be nonnegative');
    }
    return sum + item.price * item.quantity;
  }, 0);

  return Math.round(subtotal * (1 - discountPercent / 100) * 100) / 100;
}

Check it yourself:

npm run check
git diff --check
git diff

Expected after applying that fix: all 6 tests pass. Passing tests don't prove every possible behavior is correct, and git diff still needs human review. But at least we're discussing evidence instead of vibes.

The useful loop is:

Edit -> Run checks -> Read real failure -> Fix -> Run again
                                     |
                            Stop after 3 attempts
                            and request review

An agent that retries forever isn't autonomous. It's a subscription renewal strategy.

Step 6: Make the harness survive your laptop

Create .github/workflows/check.yml:

name: Check
on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
      - run: npm run check
      - run: git diff --check

Open a pull request. Now CI runs the same checks as your local agent.

For production use, pin third party GitHub Actions to vetted commit SHAs, enforce required checks and reviews, and protect tests and guardrails (for example with CODEOWNERS and branch rules). An agent can make its own evaluation look green by weakening the evaluator if you let it edit everything.

Also: run agent executed code in a suitably restricted environment. Tests don't replace sandboxing, permissions, or approval gates for destructive actions.

So what did we actually gain?

Before, your quality strategy was:

“Please be careful.”

Now you have:

Problem Harness response
Agent invents test results Run npm run check and read the actual exit code
Agent forgets project conventions AGENTS.md + architecture notes
Agent introduces forbidden imports Architectural guardrail fails
Agent breaks behavior Regression tests fail
Agent declares victory early CI and human review remain separate gates

You can also preserve longer tasks using a short docs/HANDOFF.md with the objective, files changed, real verification results, blockers, and next action. Don't paste an entire chat transcript and call it documentation.

Want to know whether this helps your team? Measure it.

Take five comparable tasks. Use the same model, starting repository state, allowed attempts, and time budget. Compare prompt-only versus prompt + harness. Track:

  • Verified task success rate.
  • Human review time.
  • Unrelated files changed.
  • Number of repair attempts.
  • Token/API cost.

Avoid pretending a single toy example proves a universal performance gain. The point of this lab is to demonstrate the mechanism, not manufacture a benchmark.

The uncomfortable conclusion

Prompt engineering isn't dead. But “write a better prompt” is not a complete software engineering strategy.

If you give an agent no tests, no context, no guardrails, and unlimited permissions, it can fail very efficiently. Congratulations: you've automated chaos.

A harness makes failure visible and gives the agent a structured chance to recover. That doesn't guarantee correctness. It gives you a way to evaluate it.

The goal isn't an agent that confidently announces:

Everything is production ready! 🚀

It's a workflow that can prove:

✓ Architecture checks passed
✓ 6 behavior tests passed
✓ Changes reviewed before merging
→ Ready for human approval

What was the last thing your AI coding agent confidently broke? And more importantly: what single automated check would have caught it?

Tell me in the comments. I collect these stories the way some people collect Pokémon.

Further reading:

  • OpenAI — Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
  • Anthropic — Effective harnesses for long-running agents
  • Google — The Anatomy of Harness Engineering
