articles.body_html:
A TinySA sweep logger, a CC1101 RSSI cross-check, and a diff script that tells you which spikes belong to your own room.

Two days ago Hackaday ran a write-up of Logan Zarov turning an LG D325 Android phone into a wideband receiver. Root, LineageOS, a modem firmware change that exposes the baseband stream, an antenna wire, and the Bluetooth radio pressed into service as a local oscillator so the thing can hear down into shortwave. A month earlier it was the ESP32's Wi-Fi block coughing up I/Q samples, then an ESP32-C5 pulling analog drone video out of 5 GHz.

The pattern is clear. Every radio chip in the junk drawer has an SDR hiding inside it, waiting for someone patient enough to find the debug path.

The part nobody posts is the boring half. A hacked receiver with an unknown front end, unknown filtering and an oscillator borrowed from a different radio will show you signals. Some of them will be real. Plenty will be its own spurs, the USB hub's switching noise, your monitor's backlight, and the LED driver in the ceiling. Before you trust anything a clever receiver tells you, you need a reference picture of your own bench, taken with an instrument whose behavior is documented.

That reference is cheap to build. Here is the one I would set up before plugging in anything exotic.

The Kit and Why Each Piece Is There

Three pieces of hardware, each with a job.

The reference instrument is a tinySA Ultra [AFFILIATE: tinySA Ultra]. It is a small swept spectrum analyzer with a USB serial console, a documented command set and a calibrated input. Calibrated matters more than sensitive here. You want a tool whose lies are written down.

The second opinion is a CC1101 module [AFFILIATE: CC1101 433 MHz SPI module] wired to an ordinary ESP32-WROOM dev board [AFFILIATE: ESP32-WROOM-32 DevKit]. The CC1101 is a sub-GHz transceiver from TI with a readable RSSI register. It has nothing in common with the tinySA's front end, which is exactly the point. When two unrelated receivers agree a signal exists, it probably does.

The third piece is a 20 dB SMA attenuator [AFFILIATE: SMA 20dB attenuator 2W]. Every spectrum analyzer has a maximum input level, and the cheapest way to kill one is a strong nearby transmitter coupled straight into the port. The attenuator also gives you a trick for spotting fake signals, covered below.

Everything here is receive-only. The CC1101 can transmit; nothing in this build asks it to.

Sweep the Room With the TinySA Over Serial

The tinySA speaks a NanoVNA-style serial console. Plug it in, and on Linux it enumerates as a CDC device, usually /dev/ttyACM0. Commands end with a carriage return, the device echoes the command, prints its output, and finishes with a ch> prompt.

The command that does the work is scan:

scan 430000000 440000000 450 2

That sweeps 430 to 440 MHz in 450 points. The final argument is an output mask; a value of 2 asks for the measured level of each point, one value per line, in dBm. The community TinySA_Python library uses the same call and parses the first whitespace-separated token of each line as the level. It also documents a firmware quirk worth guarding against: some early-2024 builds emit malformed numbers like -:.000000e+01, which the library patches before parsing.

Frequencies for each point are derived from start, stop and point count rather than read back, because the frequencies command reports the last screen sweep and follows the RBW setting, not the point count you asked for.

The logger below takes a burst of sweeps, keeps the per-bin median and per-bin maximum, and writes a baseline CSV. Install pyserial first.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""tsa_baseline.py: record or compare a tinySA spectrum baseline."""
import argparse
import csv
import statistics
import time

import serial


def command(port, line, timeout=30.0):
    port.reset_input_buffer()
    port.write((line + "\r").encode())
    buf = b""
    deadline = time.time() + timeout
    while not buf.endswith(b"ch> ") and time.time() < deadline:
        buf += port.read(port.in_waiting or 1)
    lines = buf.decode(errors="replace").splitlines()
    return [l.strip() for l in lines[1:] if l.strip() and not l.startswith("ch>")]


def parse_level(token):
    token = token.replace("-:.0", "-10.0").replace(":.0", "10.0")
    return float(token)


def sweep(port, start, stop, points):
    rows = command(port, f"scan {start} {stop} {points} 2")
    levels = [parse_level(r.split()[0]) for r in rows]
    step = (stop - start) / (points - 1)
    return [(start + i * step, lvl) for i, lvl in enumerate(levels)]


def record(args, port):
    runs = []
    for n in range(args.sweeps):
        runs.append(sweep(port, args.start, args.stop, args.points))
        print(f"sweep {n + 1}/{args.sweeps} done")
        time.sleep(args.gap)
    with open(args.file, "w", newline="") as fh:
        out = csv.writer(fh)
        out.writerow(["freq_hz", "median_dbm", "max_dbm"])
        for i in range(len(runs[0])):
            levels = [r[i][1] for r in runs]
            out.writerow([int(runs[0][i][0]),
                          round(statistics.median(levels), 1),
                          round(max(levels), 1)])
    print(f"baseline written to {args.file}")


def compare(args, port):
    with open(args.file) as fh:
        base = [(float(r["freq_hz"]), float(r["max_dbm"]))
                for r in csv.DictReader(fh)]
    now = sweep(port, args.start, args.stop, args.points)
    hot = [(f, lvl, lvl - b) for (f, lvl), (_, b) in zip(now, base)
           if lvl - b >= args.margin]
    for f, lvl, delta in hot:
        print(f"{f / 1e6:10.4f} MHz  {lvl:6.1f} dBm  +{delta:4.1f} dB over baseline max")
    if not hot:
        print("nothing above baseline max + margin")


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("mode", choices=["record", "compare"])
    ap.add_argument("--port", default="/dev/ttyACM0")
    ap.add_argument("--start", type=int, default=430_000_000)
    ap.add_argument("--stop", type=int, default=440_000_000)
    ap.add_argument("--points", type=int, default=450)
    ap.add_argument("--sweeps", type=int, default=30)
    ap.add_argument("--gap", type=float, default=2.0)
    ap.add_argument("--margin", type=float, default=6.0)
    ap.add_argument("--file", default="baseline.csv")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    with serial.Serial(args.port, 115200, timeout=0.5) as port:
        print(command(port, "version"))
        record(args, port) if args.mode == "record" else compare(args, port)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it like this:

$ pip install pyserial
$ python3 tsa_baseline.py record --sweeps 30 --file bench_433_night.csv
$ python3 tsa_baseline.py compare --file bench_433_night.csv --margin 6

The design choice that matters is comparing against the baseline maximum, not the median. Your room is not quiet. It breathes. A switching supply that wanders in and out every few seconds will show up in some sweeps and not others, and a median-based comparison flags it every time it reappears. Comparing against the worst the room did during the baseline means the script only speaks up when something exceeds the room's own bad behavior by your margin.

Record more than one baseline. Night and day differ. So does "laptop on charger" versus "laptop on battery." Label the files honestly and keep them.

The Attenuator Test for Signals That Aren't There

Swept analyzers built from mixers generate images and spurs, and cheap ones generate more. The tinySA documentation spends real time on this, and the firmware has settings aimed at it. You can also catch a fake signal with nothing but the attenuator and arithmetic.

Take a sweep with the antenna connected directly. Insert the 20 dB attenuator and sweep again. A real external signal drops by 20 dB, give or take the attenuator's tolerance. A spur generated inside the instrument by a strong signal overloading the mixer does something different: intermodulation products fall faster than the signals that create them, so a third-order product drops by roughly three times the attenuation. Internal spurs that come from the analyzer's own oscillators barely move at all.

That gives you a sorting rule:

drops ~20 dB    -> external signal, keep it
drops far more  -> overload product, your front end is lying under load
barely moves    -> internal spur, belongs to the instrument

Run compare against an attenuated baseline and an unattenuated one, and the differences tell you which entries in your hot list are worth chasing. This same test works on the rooted phone, the ESP32 SDR, or any receiver whose filtering you can't see. It's the cheapest calibration move in radio.

A Second Opinion From the CC1101 Registers

A spectrum analyzer gives you the shape. The CC1101 gives you a vote from a completely different signal chain. The goal is a slow RSSI sweep across the same band you baselined, printed as CSV, so you can line it up with the tinySA results.

The register facts come straight from the CC1101 definitions ESPHome ships: the frequency word lives in FREQ2/FREQ1/FREQ0 at 0x0D to 0x0F, RSSI is status register 0x34, VERSION is 0x31, the strobes are SRES 0x30, SCAL 0x33, SRX 0x34, SIDLE 0x36, the read bit is 0x80, burst is 0x40, the crystal is 26 MHz, and the RSSI step is 0.5 dB with a typical offset of 74.

Status registers share addresses with strobes, which trips up everybody once. Reading 0x34 with only the read bit set sends the SRX strobe. You must set read and burst together, 0x34 | 0xC0, to get the RSSI value back.

#include <SPI.h>

const int PIN_CS = 5;     // VSPI defaults on ESP32-WROOM: SCK 18, MISO 19, MOSI 23
const int PIN_MISO = 19;
const double XTAL_HZ = 26e6;

void select() {
  digitalWrite(PIN_CS, LOW);
  while (digitalRead(PIN_MISO)) {}  // CC1101 pulls SO low when its crystal is stable
}
void release() { digitalWrite(PIN_CS, HIGH); }

void strobe(uint8_t cmd) { select(); SPI.transfer(cmd); release(); }

void writeReg(uint8_t addr, uint8_t val) {
  select(); SPI.transfer(addr); SPI.transfer(val); release();
}

uint8_t readStatus(uint8_t addr) {
  select(); SPI.transfer(addr | 0xC0); uint8_t v = SPI.transfer(0); release();
  return v;
}

void tune(double hz) {
  uint32_t word = (uint32_t)((hz * 65536.0) / XTAL_HZ);
  strobe(0x36);                       // SIDLE
  writeReg(0x0D, (word >> 16) & 0xFF);
  writeReg(0x0E, (word >> 8) & 0xFF);
  writeReg(0x0F, word & 0xFF);
  strobe(0x33);                       // SCAL: calibrate synthesizer at the new frequency
  delay(1);
  strobe(0x34);                       // SRX
  delay(3);                           // let RSSI settle
}

float rssiDbm() {
  uint8_t raw = readStatus(0x34);
  float v = (raw >= 128) ? (raw - 256) / 2.0 : raw / 2.0;
  return v - 74.0;
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(PIN_CS, OUTPUT);
  release();
  SPI.begin();
  SPI.beginTransaction(SPISettings(4000000, MSBFIRST, SPI_MODE0));
  strobe(0x30);                       // SRES
  delay(10);
  uint8_t ver = readStatus(0x31);
  Serial.printf("# CC1101 VERSION=0x%02X\n", ver);
  if (ver == 0x00 || ver == 0xFF) Serial.println("# check wiring, SPI is not talking");
  Serial.println("freq_hz,rssi_dbm");
}

void loop() {
  for (double f = 433.05e6; f <= 434.79e6; f += 25e3) {
    tune(f);
    Serial.printf("%.0f,%.1f\n", f, rssiDbm());
  }
  delay(2000);
}

At 433.92 MHz the frequency word works out to 0x10B071, which you will recognize from half the CC1101 configs on GitHub. If your output shows that tuning landing somewhere else, your crystal is not 26 MHz or your arithmetic is off.

Three honest limitations. The reset-default channel filter is roughly 200 kHz wide, so stepping at 25 kHz oversamples and smears narrow carriers across several bins. The 74 dB offset is a typical figure; TI's datasheet lists offsets that shift with data rate, so treat absolute dBm values as approximate and trust the relative shape. And the spin-wait on MISO is how TI's own timing diagram says to wait for chip-ready, but a dead module will hang the loop there forever. Add a timeout before you leave it unattended.

What you want from the CC1101 run is agreement in position and relative height with the tinySA hot list. A carrier the tinySA reports at 433.92 that the CC1101 also sees rising above its floor is real. A tinySA spike the CC1101 never notices, which also failed the attenuator test, belongs to the analyzer.

Reading the Room Like Evidence

Once you have the logs, the work becomes bookkeeping, and bookkeeping is where most RF hobbyists quit. Write down the time, the antenna, the attenuator state, which devices were powered, and where you were standing. A baseline without that metadata is a picture of nothing in particular.

The questions you can answer with this setup are narrower than the internet would like. You can say a signal was present at a frequency, at roughly a level, at a time, seen by two unrelated receivers. You cannot say what device made it or who owns that device. Detection is where an investigation starts, and every honest RF guide says so in some form.

If the measurement side is where you want to go deeper, the RF Inspection for Beginners: TinySA Spectrum Baseline Guide ($45) is the next step after the script above. It covers instrument setup and calibration before interpretation, picking RBW, sweep speed and max-hold for the specific question you are asking, comparing repeated observations, and documenting time, location, equipment and uncertainty so a sweep turns into a record. That last part is exactly what the Python skips.

If the CC1101 half grabbed you, the registers go a long way past FREQ and RSSI. Bandwidth, deviation, data rate and the AGC all change what that RSSI number means. The CC1101 Deep Dive: Register-Level RF Lab Guide ($35) works through registers, modulation, timing, deviation and noise-floor behavior on ESP32 hardware, receive-only, with a bench workflow for comparing presets against measured parameters. It's the natural follow-on once you want the second-opinion receiver tuned for the signal instead of left on reset defaults.

Then Go Play With the Clever Receivers

Now the phone hacks and ESP32 SDRs get interesting, because you have something to measure them against. Point the hacked receiver at the same band, run the same sweep schedule, and compare its hot list to your two references. Every peak it reports that your references can't confirm is a fact about the hacked receiver, its oscillator, its filtering, its firmware. That's a better result than a pretty waterfall. It is a characterization, and characterizations are what turn a clever hack into a usable instrument.

The receiver that impresses you on day one is rarely the one you trust on day thirty. The one you trust is the one whose lies you have already written down.

Sources: Hackaday, "From Phone, To SDR, No Extra Hardware" (Nov 9, 2026); Hackaday ESP32 tag (ESP32-C5 5 GHz drone video, Oct 20, 2026; ESP32 SDR frequency limits, Oct 15, 2026); LC-Linkous/TinySA_Python README; ESPHome cc1101defs.h; TI CC1101 product page.

articles.body_html:
Introduction

Every application we use—from online shopping platforms and banking apps to social media websites—depends on databases to store and manage information.

But not all databases work in the same way. Some organize information into structured tables, while others offer more flexible ways to store different types of data. This is where two popular database approaches come in: SQL and NoSQL.

If you are learning software development or planning to build an application, understanding SQL vs NoSQL is an important starting point. Both technologies help manage data, but they differ in how they organize information, handle relationships, scale, and support application requirements.

So, which one should you choose? Let's explore how each database works, its advantages, limitations, and the situations where it makes the most sense.

What Is an SQL Database?

SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is a language used to communicate with relational database management systems (RDBMS).

SQL databases store information in tables made up of rows and columns. Each table represents a particular category of information, and relationships can be created between tables.

For example, an online shopping application might have separate tables for customers, products, and orders. These tables can be connected to retrieve information such as which customer purchased a particular product.

Popular SQL database systems include:

  • MySQL
  • PostgreSQL
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • Oracle Database

How Do SQL Databases Work?

SQL databases generally follow a predefined structure called a schema. Before storing information, developers define the tables, columns, data types, and relationships.

For example, a customer table might contain:

Customer ID Name Email
101 Arun arun@example.com
102 Priya priya@example.com

When information needs to be added, updated, deleted, or retrieved, developers use SQL queries.

A simple query might look like this:

SELECT * FROM Customers;

This command retrieves all records from the Customers table.

Because data is organized into related tables, SQL databases are particularly useful when applications need structured information, reliable transactions, and complex queries.

Key Features of SQL Databases

1. Structured Data

SQL databases organize information into tables with defined columns and data types. This makes data easier to manage and retrieve.

2. Predefined Schema

The database structure is generally defined before data is stored. This helps maintain consistency across records.

3. ACID Transactions

Many relational databases support ACID properties, which help ensure reliable transactions:

  • Atomicity: A transaction is completed entirely or not at all.
  • Consistency: A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions are managed so they do not interfere improperly.
  • Durability: Once a transaction is committed, its changes are preserved even after a system failure.

4. Powerful Querying

SQL makes it possible to retrieve information from multiple related tables, filter records, calculate values, and generate reports.

5. Established Ecosystem

SQL has been widely used for decades. Developers have access to extensive documentation, tools, learning resources, and community support.

What Is a NoSQL Database?

NoSQL stands for Not Only SQL. It refers to a group of non-relational database systems designed to handle different types of data and application requirements.

Unlike traditional relational databases, NoSQL databases do not rely exclusively on tables and predefined relationships. Depending on the database type, information can be stored as documents, key-value pairs, columns, or graph structures.

This flexibility can be useful when applications handle large amounts of changing, semi-structured, or unstructured information.

Popular NoSQL databases include:

  • MongoDB
  • Redis
  • Apache Cassandra
  • Neo4j
  • Couchbase

How Do NoSQL Databases Work?

NoSQL databases use different data models depending on their purpose.

For example, a document database such as MongoDB can store information in JSON-like documents. A customer record might look like this:

{
  "customer_id": 101,
  "name": "Arun",
  "email": "arun@example.com",
  "interests": ["technology", "shopping"]
}

The document structure can be flexible, allowing different records to contain different fields when the database design permits it.

This makes NoSQL databases useful for applications where information changes frequently or does not fit neatly into traditional relational tables.

Main Types of NoSQL Databases

NoSQL databases generally fall into four major categories.

1. Document Databases

These databases store information in document formats, often using JSON-like structures.

They are useful for applications such as content management systems, product catalogs, and user profiles.

Examples: MongoDB and Couchbase.

2. Key-Value Databases

These databases store information as pairs of keys and values. Each key identifies a particular value, making this model suitable for quick lookups.

They are commonly used for caching, session management, and temporary application data.

Example: Redis.

3. Wide-Column Databases

These databases organize information into rows and flexible column families. They are designed to handle large distributed datasets and specific high-volume workloads.

Example: Apache Cassandra.

4. Graph Databases

Graph databases store information as nodes and relationships, making it easier to explore connections between different pieces of data.

They are useful for social networks, recommendation systems, and relationship analysis.

Example: Neo4j.

Key Features of NoSQL Databases

1. Flexible Data Models

NoSQL databases support different ways of organizing information. This can make them suitable for applications with changing data requirements.

2. Flexible Schema Options

Many NoSQL databases allow records to have different structures. This can reduce the need to define every field in advance.

3. Horizontal Scalability

Several NoSQL systems are designed to distribute data and workloads across multiple servers. This can help applications grow as traffic and data volumes increase.

4. Different Performance Options

NoSQL databases can be optimized for particular access patterns, such as quick key-based lookups, document retrieval, or graph traversal.

5. Multiple Database Models

Developers can choose a database model based on the kind of information their application needs to manage.

SQL vs NoSQL: Key Differences Explained

Now that we understand both database types, let's compare them across the areas that matter most.

Feature SQL Databases NoSQL Databases
Database Model Relational Non-relational
Data Organization Tables, rows, and columns Documents, key-value pairs, columns, or graphs
Schema Generally predefined Often flexible or dynamic
Relationships Supports relationships between tables Relationships are handled differently depending on the database
Transactions Strong support for complex transactions Transaction support varies by database
Scalability Commonly scaled vertically; some support horizontal scaling Many systems are designed for horizontal scaling
Data Consistency Commonly supports strong consistency Consistency models vary
Query Language SQL Depends on the database system
Examples MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Neo4j
Common Uses Banking, inventory, and transactional applications Content platforms, caching, distributed applications, and graph-based systems

The important thing to remember is that these are general differences, not strict rules for every database. Modern SQL and NoSQL systems have evolved, and their capabilities can overlap.

When Should You Use an SQL Database?

SQL databases are a strong choice when your application needs structured data, reliable transactions, and relationships between different records.

Here are some common situations where SQL makes sense.

1. Banking and Financial Applications

Financial applications need reliable transactions. When money is transferred between accounts, the system must ensure that the transaction is completed correctly.

SQL databases are commonly used for applications that require this level of transactional reliability.

2. E-Commerce Platforms

An online shopping platform manages customers, products, orders, payments, and inventory. These records are connected, so relational databases can help organize and retrieve the information efficiently.

3. Business Management Systems

Applications that manage employee records, payroll, invoices, and inventory often benefit from structured data and relationships between tables.

4. Applications That Need Complex Queries

If an application needs detailed reports, data filtering, calculations, or information from multiple related tables, SQL provides powerful querying capabilities.

5. Systems Where Data Integrity Matters

When maintaining accurate and consistent records is a priority, relational databases offer useful constraints and transaction features.

When Should You Use a NoSQL Database?

NoSQL databases are useful when an application needs a flexible data model, a particular type of data access, or distributed storage.

Here are some common use cases.

1. Social Media Applications

Social media platforms handle user profiles, posts, comments, activity, and other types of frequently changing information. Certain NoSQL database models can help manage these varied data structures.

2. Real-Time Applications

Applications that process frequent updates, such as live activity feeds or gaming platforms, may benefit from NoSQL systems designed for specific high-throughput workloads.

3. Content Management Systems

A document database can be useful when content items have different fields or structures. For example, a blog post, product page, and news article may not require exactly the same information.

4. Caching and Session Management

Key-value databases such as Redis are commonly used to store frequently accessed information, helping applications retrieve it quickly.

5. Large Distributed Applications

Some NoSQL databases are designed to distribute data across multiple servers. This can be useful for applications that need to handle growing data volumes and workloads across different locations.

Can You Use SQL and NoSQL Together?

Yes. In fact, some applications use both SQL and NoSQL databases to manage different types of information.

This approach is often called polyglot persistence.

Consider an e-commerce platform:

  • An SQL database can manage customer accounts, orders, payments, and inventory transactions.
  • A NoSQL document database can store flexible product information.
  • A key-value database can handle caching and user sessions.

Each database serves a particular purpose.

Using both does not automatically make an application better, though. Developers must consider the additional complexity of managing multiple databases, keeping information consistent, and maintaining the overall system.

The best choice depends on the application's actual requirements.

SQL vs NoSQL: Which One Is Better for Beginners to Learn?

If you are starting your journey in software development, learning SQL is a practical first step.

SQL introduces important database concepts such as tables, relationships, queries, filtering, and data management. These fundamentals are useful across many software development and data-related roles.

Once you understand relational databases, exploring NoSQL will help you understand how modern applications manage flexible and distributed data.

If you are looking to develop practical software development skills and build a strong foundation for a career in IT, exploring structured learning opportunities can be a valuable next step. REDYELLOW Technologies offers IT training and career-focused learning opportunities for aspiring technology professionals.

A useful learning path is:

  1. Understand database fundamentals.
  2. Learn tables, rows, columns, and relationships.
  3. Practice basic SQL commands such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.
  4. Learn joins, filtering, and aggregate functions.
  5. Explore a relational database such as MySQL or PostgreSQL.
  6. Understand NoSQL concepts and explore MongoDB.
  7. Build a small project that uses a database to store and retrieve information.

The best way to understand databases is to work with real examples rather than simply memorizing definitions.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is the main difference between SQL and NoSQL?

SQL databases use a relational model that organizes information into tables. NoSQL databases use different data models, including documents, key-value pairs, wide columns, and graphs.

2. Is SQL better than NoSQL?

Neither is always better. SQL is often suitable for structured data and applications requiring complex transactions. NoSQL can be a better fit for flexible data models and certain distributed workloads. The right choice depends on the project.

3. Is MongoDB a SQL or NoSQL database?

MongoDB is a NoSQL database. It uses a document-based model to store information in flexible, JSON-like documents.

4. Can SQL databases handle large amounts of data?

Yes. Modern SQL databases can manage large datasets and support different scaling strategies. Their performance depends on database design, hardware, queries, and workload.

5. Can SQL and NoSQL be used in the same application?

Yes. An application can use SQL for transactional records and NoSQL for other requirements, such as flexible documents or caching. This is known as polyglot persistence.

6. Should beginners learn SQL or NoSQL first?

SQL is a useful starting point because it teaches fundamental database concepts. After learning SQL, beginners can explore NoSQL systems such as MongoDB to understand alternative data models.

Conclusion

SQL and NoSQL databases both play important roles in modern application development. They solve different data management challenges, and choosing between them depends on the way an application stores, processes, and retrieves information.

SQL is a strong option for structured data, relational queries, and reliable transactions. NoSQL offers different data models that can support flexible structures and distributed workloads.

Instead of focusing on which database is more popular, developers should understand what their application actually needs. Learning both approaches provides a stronger foundation for building and managing modern software applications.

For anyone entering the technology field, understanding database fundamentals is a valuable step toward becoming a more capable developer.

articles.title: 0.1 + 0.2 Is Not a Bug. It's Arithmetic in a Costume.
articles.description: The first time 0.30000000000000004 showed up on my screen I did what everyone does. I blamed Python....
articles.body_html:
The first time 0.30000000000000004 showed up on my screen I did what everyone does. I blamed Python. Then I blamed my keyboard. Then Python again, louder.

It's not Python. JavaScript prints the same number, and so does nearly every language on your machine, because nearly every language stores decimals the same way: as IEEE 754 doubles, a standard from 1985 that is older than most of the people complaining about it.

Where does the extra 4 come from?

Write one third as a decimal. You can't. You get 0.333 and then the 3s keep going until you run out of patience or paper, and whatever you eventually write down is close to a third but is not a third.

Binary has the same problem with different numbers. 0.1 in binary is 0.0001100110011..., the "0011" repeating forever. A double gives you 53 bits of precision to store that with, so the machine stores the closest value it can fit and moves on.

You can see the stand-in Python actually uses:

from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal(0.1))

Output:

0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

That's the 0.1 your computer owns. 0.2 is a different approximation with a different tail. Add the two stand-ins and the errors come along for the ride:

print(0.1 + 0.2)

0.30000000000000004

Nobody made an error in the addition. The addition is exact. It's exact arithmetic performed on inexact numbers, which is a different and much more annoying sentence.

Does it get worse if you keep adding?

Yes, politely.

total = 0.0
for x in [0.1] * 10:
    total += x
print(total)

0.9999999999999999

Ten copies of almost-0.1, added one at a time, each rounding nudging the pile. Amusing footnote: Python 3.12's built-in sum() returns exactly 1.0 for this, because it now uses compensated summation that tracks the lost crumbs. The plain loop doesn't. When a language starts quietly patching around a problem, that's your sign the problem is everywhere.

When should you actually care?

Two situations. The first is equality. 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False, and any code that compares floats with == is a landmine with a countdown you can't read. Compare with a tolerance instead:

import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

True

The second is money, and this one I take personally. I sell a small digital product priced at $7.99 and work out revenue per visitor in a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet runs on the same doubles. At my scale, a floating point error is a ghost worth a ten-thousandth of a cent and I lose no sleep over it. But the fix costs nothing, so the rule in my notebook is absolute: money is counted in integers of the smallest unit, 799 cents, or in Decimal. Never in floats.

Decimal does base-10 arithmetic, the kind money is actually denominated in:

from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2'))

Decimal('0.3')

Note the quotes. Decimal(0.1), no quotes, builds the decimal out of the binary float, and you already saw what that contains. Feeding Decimal a float is mopping the floor with the muddy water. Strings in, exact decimals out.

JavaScript gets no separate treatment here, because there's nothing to treat. Its numbers are the same doubles:

console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);

false

Same standard, same costume, same party.

The part nobody puts on the poster

Floats are not a scam. For graphics, physics, machine learning, anything where the input was an approximation to begin with, a double is fast, hardware-supported, and accurate far beyond what the measurement deserved. The honest catch is that Decimal is slower and grumpier to write, and reaching for it everywhere is its own kind of cargo cult. The sin was never using floats. The sin is using them in the two places they're guaranteed to embarrass you: equality checks and cash.

Every senior dev I've watched hit this has the same story shape. The demo worked. The tests worked. Then the system ran a few million operations, the errors held hands, and a total came out one cent or one vote or one millisecond wrong, and somebody got to spend a Friday finding out why.

Where did floating point last bite you? I want the specific version, the one with the Friday in it.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: The Array Hiding in Every params Call
articles.description: A four-line display-name helper was quietly allocating an array on every call through params T[]. Switching to C# 13's params ReadOnlySpan<T> took it from 107 MB to zero, with the call sites unchanged.
articles.body_html:
I was reading a gen0 allocation profile for a service that does almost nothing interesting, and sitting near the top was a four-line helper I'd written months ago and never thought about again. It picks a display name: try the nickname, fall back to the full name, fall back to the email, fall back to "Anonymous". It allocates nothing of its own. Or so I assumed. It was handing the garbage collector an array on every single call, and I never passed it one.

Here's the helper, more or less as it was:

static string FirstNonEmpty(params string?[] parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p))
            return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}

And the call site, which runs once per request:

string name = FirstNonEmpty(user.Nickname, user.FullName, user.Email, "Anonymous");

That looks like I'm passing four strings. What I'm actually doing is asking the compiler to build a string?[4], drop those four references into it, and hand the array to the method. params T[] has worked that way since C# 1. Every call with inline arguments mints a fresh array, uses it for a few nanoseconds, and throws it away. The strings themselves already exist and get reused; the array is pure packaging.

Measuring the packaging

I don't trust my gut on allocation sizes, so I measured it with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around a tight loop rather than a stopwatch. Allocation counts are deterministic, so the number doesn't drift between runs the way milliseconds do. Two million calls, rotating through a few fake users so the branch isn't always the same:

.NET 10.0.15, 2,000,000 calls each

params string?[]                106.8 MB  gen0=0  (checksum 18000000)

107 MB of arrays to pick a name two million times. Each array is only about 56 bytes, but 56 bytes times two million is real, and in a service choosing a display name on every request it's a steady drip, not a one-off.

I want to be honest about one thing in that output: gen0=0. The collector hadn't fired during my measured window, because this box has a roomy ephemeral budget and 107 MB didn't fill it. So this isn't a GC-pauses horror story. The garbage is real, it just hadn't been swept yet. On a busy box with a tighter budget, that's exactly the kind of drip that turns into gen0 collections you actually feel.

The one-word fix

C# 13 added params collections, and the one I reach for is params ReadOnlySpan<T>. Change the parameter type and nothing else:

static string FirstNonEmpty(params ReadOnlySpan<string?> parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p))
            return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}

The call site doesn't change at all. FirstNonEmpty(user.Nickname, user.FullName, user.Email, "Anonymous") compiles the same way it reads. But now the compiler stack-allocates the arguments instead of newing up an array, because the span doesn't escape the call. Same loop, same inputs, same checksum:

params ReadOnlySpan<string?>      0.0 MB  gen0=0  (checksum 18000000)

Zero. The strings are still there, the result is identical, and the packaging is gone. The timing moved too, though I trust it less than the allocation number. Best of five runs in the same cloud container, I care about the ratio and not the absolute milliseconds:

array  : 36 ms (best of 5)
span   : 8 ms (best of 5)

Most of that gap is the allocation work itself plus the collections the array version triggers across repeated runs. In a real service you'd never see a clean 4x, but you would see the arrays disappear, and that part is deterministic.

When I'd leave it alone

This isn't a reason to go sed your whole codebase. The win only shows up when the arguments are passed inline at the call site, so the compiler can see they don't escape. If your callers already have a List<string> or a string[] in hand and pass that, you were never allocating a throwaway array, and a ReadOnlySpan<T> overload buys you nothing there. It also does nothing for boxing: if the parameter is params ReadOnlySpan<object> and you pass ints, each int still boxes onto the heap, array or not. And on a path that runs a few hundred times a day, none of this matters and I wouldn't touch it.

My honest opinion: for a hot-path helper you control, params ReadOnlySpan<T> is close to free money, because the call sites don't change and the signature reads the same. For a public API, I'd think harder, since a span parameter can't be captured in an async method or a lambda, and that constraint leaks to your callers.

Here's the whole thing I ran, if you want to reproduce it:

using System.Diagnostics;

static string FirstNonEmptyArray(params string?[] parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p)) return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}

static string FirstNonEmptySpan(params ReadOnlySpan<string?> parts)
{
    foreach (var p in parts)
        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p)) return p;
    return "Anonymous";
}

const int N = 2_000_000;
string?[] nick = [null, "", "jpeg_enjoyer", null, "  "];
string?[] full = ["Dana Okoro", null, "Lee Park", "", "Mina Roy"];
string?[] mail = ["dana@x.io", "sam@x.io", "lee@x.io", "al@x.io", "mina@x.io"];

static long RunArray(string?[] a, string?[] b, string?[] c, int n)
{
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
        int k = i % 5;
        sum += FirstNonEmptyArray(a[k], b[k], c[k], "Anonymous").Length;
    }
    return sum;
}

static long RunSpan(string?[] a, string?[] b, string?[] c, int n)
{
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
        int k = i % 5;
        sum += FirstNonEmptySpan(a[k], b[k], c[k], "Anonymous").Length;
    }
    return sum;
}

RunArray(nick, full, mail, 10_000);   // warm up
RunSpan(nick, full, mail, 10_000);

long Measure(string label, Func<long> run)
{
    GC.Collect();
    GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
    GC.Collect();
    int g0 = GC.CollectionCount(0);
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    long checksum = run();
    long bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
    Console.WriteLine($"{label,-28} {bytes / 1024.0 / 1024.0,8:F1} MB  gen0={GC.CollectionCount(0) - g0}  (checksum {checksum})");
    return bytes;
}

Console.WriteLine($".NET {Environment.Version}, {N:N0} calls each\n");
Measure("params string?[]", () => RunArray(nick, full, mail, N));
Measure("params ReadOnlySpan<string?>", () => RunSpan(nick, full, mail, N));

Have you found one of these hiding in your own hot path, or is there a params call you'd never convert because the callers always hand it an array already? I'd like to hear which side you land on.

— still benchmarking helpers nobody asked me to profile

articles.title: Python Just Got a New Kind of String. It Could End a Whole Class of Security Bugs.
articles.description: t-strings (PEP 750) are the biggest change to Python string formatting since f-strings, and they exist for one reason. f-strings cannot be made safe.
articles.body_html:
t-strings (PEP 750) are the biggest change to Python string formatting since f-strings, and they exist for one reason: f-strings cannot be made safe. Here is what they are and why they matter.

Every SQL injection, every cross-site scripting hole, every shell-injection bug has the same shape at its heart. Somebody took a piece of untrusted input and glued it directly into a string that was then treated as code, as a query, as markup. The input became structure instead of data.

query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"

If name is O'Brien, the apostrophe closes the quoted value early and the query breaks. If name is crafted by an attacker, the same mechanism lets them add their own commands to your query.

The f-string did exactly what it was designed to do: take the value and put it in the string. Immediately. Finished. And that immediacy is precisely the problem. By the time you have the string, the dangerous value is already welded into it, indistinguishable from the safe parts. There is no seam left to escape.

Python 3.14 introduced a new kind of string literal, standardized in PEP 750, built specifically to fix this. They are called t-strings (template strings), and as the Python 3.15 world settles in late 2026, they are the most consequential change to string handling since f-strings arrived.

Here is what they are, how they differ from f-strings in one crucial way, and why that difference can close an entire category of vulnerabilities.

The One Difference That Changes Everything

A t-string looks almost exactly like an f-string. Same braces, same interpolation syntax. The only visible change is the prefix: t instead of f.

name = "Pythonista"
greeting = t"Hello, {name}!"

But the result is completely different in the way that matters. An f-string evaluates to a finished str. A t-string evaluates to a Template object, from the new string.templatelib module. Not a string. A structured object.

type(t"Hello, {name}!")
# <class 'string.templatelib.Template'>

And here is the heart of it.

  • An f-string does the interpolation eagerly. It grabs the value of name, drops it into the text, and hands you a done string with no memory of which parts were literal and which came from a variable.
  • A t-string does not interpolate into a final string at all. Instead, it keeps the pieces separate: the static text parts on one side, the interpolated values on the other, handed to you as a structured object you can inspect and process before anything becomes a finished string.

The f-string gives you the result. The t-string gives you the recipe, with the dangerous ingredients still in their own labeled containers, so a library can treat them differently from the trusted parts before combining them.

What a Template Actually Holds

Because a Template keeps the pieces apart, you can look at them. It exposes its structure directly:

name = "Pythonista"
site = "example.dev"
template = t"Hello, {name}! Welcome to {site}!"

template.strings
# ('Hello, ', '! Welcome to ', '!')      <- the static text parts

template.values
# ('Pythonista', 'example.dev')           <- the interpolated values

template.interpolations
# (Interpolation('Pythonista', 'name', ...), Interpolation('example.dev', 'site', ...))

Three things to notice:

  • .strings holds the literal text fragments you typed, the parts that are always safe because you wrote them. There is always exactly one more static string than there are interpolations (the text before, between, and after the holes).
  • .interpolations holds the dynamic parts, each as an Interpolation object. Each Interpolation carries not just the .value (the actual runtime value, 'Pythonista') but also the .expression (the source text you wrote in the braces, 'name'), plus the conversion and format spec.
  • The value and the literal text are kept in completely separate buckets.

You can also just iterate the template, and it alternates between static strings and Interpolation objects in order:

from string.templatelib import Interpolation

for part in template:
    if isinstance(part, Interpolation):
        ...  # a dynamic value, treat it as untrusted
    else:
        ...  # a static string, trusted, you wrote it

That loop is the key. It lets code walk through the template and do one thing to the parts you wrote and a different thing to the parts that came from outside. That is exactly the distinction every injection bug fails to make.

The Safety Payoff, Concretely

Here is why this matters, shown with HTML and the classic cross-site scripting problem. To keep the example simple, imagine a user submits markup where plain text was expected.

With an f-string, untrusted input goes straight into the page, raw:

user_input = "<b>injected markup</b>"
f"<p>{user_input}</p>"
# "<p><b>injected markup</b></p>"

The f-string is already a finished string, and the user's tags are now live markup, exactly as if you had written them yourself. It is too late to escape; you cannot tell anymore which angle brackets you wrote and which came from the user. In a real attack, those tags would carry a script instead of bold text.

With a t-string, you hand the Template to a function that walks it and escapes only the interpolated values, leaving your static markup untouched:

from html import escape
from string.templatelib import Template, Interpolation

def to_safe_html(tpl: Template) -> str:
    out = []
    for part in tpl:
        if isinstance(part, Interpolation):
            out.append(escape(str(part.value), quote=True))   # untrusted: escape it
        else:
            out.append(part)                                   # trusted: your own text
    return "".join(out)

bad = "<script>alert('x')</script>"
to_safe_html(t"<p>{bad}</p>")
# '<p><script>alert('x')</script></p>'   <- neutralized

The interpolated value is treated as untrusted and escaped, while the static text is your own and passes through unchanged. The user's tags are now harmless visible text, while your <p> tags pass through intact.

One writer put the principle perfectly: the escaper "sees user input as user input, not as a string fragment."

Now generalize. The same pattern applies everywhere injection lives:

  • A SQL library can take a t-string and turn every interpolation into a bound parameter instead of concatenated text, which removes the main route for injection.
  • A shell library can quote every interpolated argument.
  • A logging library can redact.

In each case the library gets to decide how to handle the dynamic parts because they arrived separately, which is the one thing f-strings never allow.

The Deliberate Inconvenience: A Template Is Not a String

There is a design choice in t-strings that looks like a limitation and is actually the point. A Template does not render itself into a string by default. You cannot just use it where a string is expected.

  • Printing one shows its repr, not interpolated text.
  • You cannot add a plain string to a Template with + (that raises TypeError; only Template + Template is allowed).
  • It has no len().

It genuinely is not a string, and it refuses to pretend to be one.

print(t"Hello, {name}!")
# Template(strings=('Hello, ', '!'), interpolations=(Interpolation('Pythonista', 'name', None, ''),))

That is the structured object, not the text "Hello, Pythonista!".

This feels annoying until you see why. If a Template quietly turned itself into a string the moment you used it carelessly, it would reintroduce the exact danger it exists to prevent: an un-escaped interpolation sliding into output because someone forgot to process it.

By requiring that every template be run through a processing function before it becomes text, the design makes "forgot to escape" much harder. You cannot accidentally use the raw version, because the raw version is not usable as a string.

The inconvenience is a guardrail.

So t-strings do not escape anything on their own. They are the mechanism that lets a library escape safely. The t-string carries the pieces, apart and inspectable; the library does the right thing with them. What Python standardized is the shape, so every library can speak it.

The Rule I Take Away

Compressed to one line:

An f-string interpolates eagerly into a finished str, fusing trusted text and untrusted values together with no seam left to escape, which is why it is unsafe for SQL, HTML, and shell. A t-string produces a Template that keeps the static parts (.strings) and the interpolated values (.interpolations, each with .value) separate, so a library can escape or parameterize the untrusted parts before building the final string.

The deeper lesson, the one that outlasts this specific feature, is that safety against injection comes from preserving the boundary between structure and data for as long as possible.

Every injection vulnerability is a place where that boundary was erased too early, where a value became part of the sentence before anyone could treat it as a value. F-strings erase the boundary instantly, by design, because they were built for convenience, not safety. T-strings keep the boundary intact and hand it to you, which is what finally lets Python libraries offer "safe by construction" interpolation the way other ecosystems have with tagged templates.

And the practical reality as of today: t-strings are new (3.14, carried into the 3.15 world), and the libraries that consume them are still growing. You will not rewrite everything overnight. But the direction is set, and when a SQL, HTML, or shell library offers a t-string API, reaching for it instead of an f-string is one of the cheapest security upgrades you can make.

What to Actually Do With This

Concrete guidance for where t-strings are right now:

Situation Use Why
Logging a number, debug messages, formatting output you control f-strings Perfect there and not going anywhere. The problem is only ever untrusted input crossing into code, query, or markup.
SQL queries, HTML output, shell commands with values you didn't write t-strings + t-string-aware libraries That is the boundary t-strings were built to protect.

And two standing rules:

  • Never build SQL, HTML, or shell commands with f-strings and raw interpolation. This was always true; t-strings now give you a first-class, standard alternative instead of only "remember to use parameterized queries / escape manually."
  • Watch for t-string support in your libraries. As database drivers, template engines, and shell helpers add t-string APIs, prefer them. The whole value of PEP 750 is a single standard shape that every library can accept, so the ecosystem can make the safe path the easy path.

Python did not just add a nicer way to format strings. It added a way to hand libraries the raw ingredients of a string with the dangerous ones still labeled, so they can be made safe before serving. That is a small syntax change pointed at one of the oldest and most damaging categories of bug in software.

The 30-Second Takeaway

  • t-strings (PEP 750, Python 3.14+) look like f-strings but use a t prefix and evaluate to a Template object (string.templatelib), not a str.
  • The key difference: an f-string interpolates eagerly into a finished string, fusing your text and the values together with no way left to escape them. A t-string keeps the pieces separate for you to process first.
  • A Template exposes its structure: .strings (the static text you wrote, always one more than the values), .interpolations (each an Interpolation with .value the runtime value and .expression the source text), and .values. Iterating it alternates static strings and interpolations.
  • The security payoff: a library can walk the template and escape or parameterize only the interpolated (untrusted) values, leaving your static markup or query intact, before building the string. This removes the main route for SQL injection, XSS, and shell injection.
  • A Template is deliberately not a string: no default render, adding a plain string with + raises TypeError, no len(). This forces you to process it, so you cannot accidentally emit un-escaped output. The inconvenience is a guardrail.
  • t-strings do not escape by themselves; they are the standard mechanism that lets libraries escape safely. Use f-strings for safe internal formatting; use t-strings (and t-string-aware libraries) wherever untrusted input meets SQL, HTML, or shell.

Your Turn

Find one place in your code where you build SQL, HTML, or a shell command with an f-string and an interpolated value you did not write. That is an injection risk today. As your libraries add t-string support, that exact spot is where the t prefix becomes the cheapest security fix you will ever ship.

Have you tried t-strings yet? What's the first place you'd use them? Tell me in the comments 👇

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.
